toc.title: A safe space is not the same as feeling safe
When you're part of the problem
What I saw in my cohorts
You don't have to be a doormat
Someone has to do something different
Two: focus on small, consistent safety cues
Three: stop trying to fix your spouse
Four: validate the feeling, not necessarily the content

blocks.p: When your spouse is dysregulated and shut down, and then lashes out in anger, what's happening, and what can you do about it? The extremely short version of what to do about it is to stay regulated yourself. The longer discussion is around responsibility and boundaries. I'll address all of this and more.

I got an email I'm going to respond to. I'm responding generally, not directly to this person, and this is not personal life advice. But I think a lot of people can relate to this listener's question. Here's a condensed version of it:

q: Thank you for your material on dorsal vagal shutdown. It's helped me understand what my wife is going through. However, I can't find anything on what I can do to better help her as her spouse. I know I need to be a better anchor. Unfortunately, I think much of her shutdown is due to marital problems, which has led her to shutting me out. I want to be there for her and prove I can be her anchor, but it's hard. When she sometimes lashes out with anger, I know it's a sign she's coming out of shutdown, but then she slips right back in. I just don't know what to do.

blocks.p: First off, thank you so much for the email and the really great question. The core of it boils down to one of the most difficult questions in any relationship: how do I help somebody I love when they're stuck in a defensive state?

But there are other questions embedded here too. What's my role? What's my responsibility to my partner? What's a safety anchor? Can a spouse be a safety anchor? What if they have not been one in the past? There's a lot to get into.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: A safe space is not the same as feeling safe

blocks.p: The listener mentions an important distinction. He says there's no abuse, violence, or infidelity, so she is in a safe space. Logically this makes perfect sense. He's saying the objective threats are gone. And that's vital, a super important and necessary foundation. So, good job. No one should be hitting each other or being violent toward each other in any way.

But in the world of the nervous system, there's a huge difference between a space being technically safe and the actual feeling of safety, the biological reality of safety. When I talk about safety, here or with my clients, I'm not referring to literal safety. Yes, that's part of it. A safe enough environment and safe enough people are extremely important. But there's way more to it. Safety refers to biology: the ventral vagal safety pathways, from the brainstem in particular.

We need these to, in essence, activate, for lack of a better word, and the environment and the people are a part of that. But someone who lives in a chronically defensive state like shutdown has less activation of their safety pathways, and they need more than literal safety. They need to access their safety state and then practice being in it. More than once. A lot. They need to put in the safety reps and exercise their safety state, similar to working out to increase your strength or to build any sort of skill.
Part of this process is connecting with and building safety. Another part, which is way more difficult, is connecting with stuck defense.

One problem, however, is that someone who is stuck in defense has a difficult time, first, identifying safety. Second, being with it. Third, experiencing it mindfully. And fourth, building its strength. And they have a much harder time connecting with stuck defense and relieving it.

Someone who is stuck in defense will identify danger when it's not there, something we call unhealthy neuroception in the polyvagal world. So it's great that your home is free from overtly dangerous things. Keep doing that. But that doesn't mean your spouse is able to shift out of stuck defense. On top of that, your spouse may not identify you as a safety cue, especially if there's a history of issues between you.

On top of that, there may be very subtle cues of danger, or non-safety, that we give to our partners and that are very easily missed. For example, the flattened tone of voice when we get annoyed. Or a subtle eye roll as we look away. Or a pained grimace when our spouse asks us to get them something right when we sit down, every single time.

And on top of that, in relationships we tend to overly rely on the other person to be the source of our healing. Tell me I'm wrong. We enable each other's behaviors and emotions. Tell me I'm wrong. We build codependency on each other. We blame the other person, waiting for them to change, thinking that when they finally change, then we can change. Tell me I'm wrong. And the other person is waiting for us to do the same.
Point being, there are layers of stuff to deal with. Having a safe enough environment is good, and being a safe enough person is also good, but there is a lot more to it.

If I asked this person's wife, "Is your husband a safe person, a safe spouse?" she would probably say yes. If I asked, "Do you feel safe with him?" she would probably also say yes, or look at me weirdly, because people don't typically talk like this. So we have to narrow it down more. If I asked, "Do you breathe easier when you're with your husband? Do you smile? Do you want to get closer to him?" she might say no.

So the goal isn't to convince your partner's thinking brain that they are safe. The goal is to show that they're safe to be in your presence. The goal is to show that it's okay to come out of hiding, or to drop their defenses.
But again, lots of layers, and way easier said than done.

blocks.h: When you're part of the problem

blocks.p: If that's not complicated enough, here's where it gets more complicated. This listener, and maybe you can relate, says his wife's shutdown is due to marital problems. That means he's in a uniquely difficult position.

He is simultaneously a potential source of safety, and potential is the word. There's history there, there's familiarity, there's love. But he's also a potential source of threat or danger. Her nervous system may not distinguish between "He's trying to help" and "He's part of the problem." Again, this is a biological process, not a cognitive one. One spouse may know the other person is safe, but biologically, their body is not in a safety state.

Now let's address the moments of lashing out. The listener could be exactly right. It could be a sign of movement, of self-regulation. It's potentially a very good sign. Is it a good sign that she's lashing out in anger and directing it at another person? No. That is not what I mean.

We are mammals. If we can't be safe, we run. If we can't run, we fight. If we can't fight, we shut down. But we can get stuck in one of those defensive states. Someone who's stuck needs to come out of this sequence in the reverse order: from shutdown and immobilization, emerging into fight activation, then flight, and then safety. So from immobilization, to mobilization, to safety. Deb Dana calls this the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system).

So coming out of shutdown and into anger is sort of a good sign. It's a signal that the body is attempting to come out of immobilization. The body may be trying to self-regulate, to get unstuck from stuck shutdown.

But when the anger is chaotic and taken out on others, on the self, or on property, that is obviously less than ideal. It signals that the body is trying to come out of immobilization but lacks the safety capacity to handle the returning mobilization. The safety state needs to be strengthened first. As it strengthens, self-regulation becomes much more of a possibility.

blocks.h: What I saw in my cohorts

blocks.p: I've actually found this to be true in the last two cohorts I ran: Safety Simplified, a four-week one, and Self-Regulation Simplified, an eight-week one. In both cohorts, safety activation went way up, and defensive activation overall went way down, but not entirely. Fight activation increased in both cohorts.

Why would this be? Through the material, the practices, and the co-regulation among the students when we met live, the levels of safety went way up. As safety went way up, shutdown and freeze went way down. And as they went way down, fight activation went up. In other words, as the body came out of immobility, mobility increased.

But not disorganized, chaotic mobility. The cohort members shared stories where they felt empowered. They were using that mobile energy, that activation, to take on new challenges, to speak up for themselves, and to start new projects. It was not chaotic or disorganized, because the safety state had developed enough to not only decrease shutdown and freeze, but also to welcome and guide the defensive activation back into mobility.

So yes, fight activation coming out of shutdown is a potentially great sign, if it's regulated. When we take it out on others, that is not regulated. It is totally okay to speak from empowerment toward our spouses or others when things need to be said. That's different from lashing out and blaming, shaming, belittling, or humiliating. Please don't confuse those two things.
Here's what I suspect is happening in situations like this.

Partner A comes out of shutdown. The anger surfaces, and it gets directed at partner B, who of course gets hurt and reactive, even if they don't show it. Partner A picks up on that, and their nervous system says, "Not safe." Back into shutdown, along with life themes running through the mind, like "I knew it. I can't rely on partner B."
It's a painful but very predictable loop, and we'll come back to what to do about it.

The fight activation isn't the problem. Fight is showing up as anger, but it's mobilized energy finally moving, and that's progress. One problem is how it's expressed. Partner A ultimately needs to strengthen safety, and then mindfully welcome the fight activation back into the system.

Another problem is what happens next. Partner B justifiably has a reaction to partner A's anger, but lacks the regulation to do something different, just as partner A lacks the regulation. There's a rupture, or misattunement, in the biological communication between both partners, as well as behavioral and verbal miscommunication. And on top of that, there's potentially no repair happening, no return to safety together. Just the familiar aggression and then retreat, probably over and over again.

blocks.h: You don't have to be a doormat

blocks.p: If you've been on the receiving end of this cycle as partner B, your nervous system has been through it too. Being patient and caring does not mean absorbing verbal abuse indefinitely. Your biology matters. Your safety matters. Being a doormat is not anchoring, for you or for the other person.

Some people would call that fawning. I would call it codependency, or insecurity, or shutting down, or freezing. I would never ask someone in shutdown to just snap out of it, because that's not how biology works. And I'm also not going to ask their spouse to endlessly tolerate mistreatment because the other person is struggling.

That's not okay. Both things can be true: your partner is in pain, and you don't have to be their doormat or their punching bag. Partner B, the one being targeted by A's anger, can hold compassion for their struggle while also holding a boundary for themselves. In fact, boundaries are safety cues, in my opinion.

A person who can calmly say, "I hear that you're upset, and I'm not going to continue this conversation while you're talking to me this way," is demonstrating regulation. That may not feel great for partner A, and they might interpret it as abandonment or rejection, but that is ultimately partner A's problem to deal with.

Partner B can totally be a support, but not at the expense of their own wellbeing. Healthy boundaries, including an assertive refusal to participate when partner A is being hurtful, are a cue to partner A that partner B is self-regulated and a safe other. Even if it does not initially feel that way, and even if partner A initially interprets the refusal as abandonment or rejection.

If you're partner B and you've done things in the relationship you need to make amends for, you should probably hurry up and do so. If you've done something you need to apologize for, do it. And if your spouse needs to share how those choices impacted them, you need to listen, even if it hurts.

Once they start to shame and belittle, that's different. That is not okay. We need each other's co-regulation, but we can't get that when we're mistreating the other person. Mistreating others instantly puts them into a defensive state, and then co-regulation gets cut off, understandably.

And when co-regulation is cut off, we return to familiar habits of hiding, or blaming, or avoiding. And we return to familiar stories of being abandoned yet again, or being unlovable, or "I knew I could never trust you." This isn't about blame. It's biological communication between two organisms with very complex, multi-layered backgrounds. Breaking old individual and relational cycles requires a much different approach, and it's extremely difficult.

blocks.h: Someone has to do something different

blocks.p: Somebody in this pair has to do something different. Ideally, both people, A and B, confront difficult conversations only after first anchoring into their own safety state, and then come together and focus on healthy communication skills.
But that's not likely to happen, is it? It could happen, but both people need to be on the same page, and that's not typically how relationships go.
So, dear listener, it falls on you. I don't have your spouse here listening to me. I only have you. If you want your relationship dynamics to change, it's on you.
Wait, wait, wait. Don't give up on me now. Let me explain. If you show up differently, the relationship must change.

Imagine the relationship like a machine made up of only two gears. You and your spouse are the gears. The machine is the relationship. Both gears move together. Whether it's pleasant hand-holding walks on the beach or unpleasant fighting and retreating, the gears are moving together.

If one of the gears refuses to move the same way, something must change. Ideally, both gears work together to change the machine. Realistically, that's not going to happen. Even when couples show up to therapy together, it's usually one of the gears that's forcing the issue.

So is it up to you to heal the relationship? No. Is it up to you to heal your partner? Also no. Please don't hear it that way. But if you want your relationship to change, it is up to you to show up differently. You need to be the gear that refuses to move in the same way.
Yes. Heck yes, this causes more friction initially. Change always does, maybe especially in intimate partner relationships.

If I had you in the therapy room with your spouse, I would easily put it on both of you. But I probably have only one of you, one of the gears in the machine, and so it's on you to do something differently, because you're the one hearing it.
You need to be, first and foremost, self-regulated. If you can be self-regulated, you can act as your partner's co-regulator. You can be their anchor, and the catalyst for change in the relationship.

"But Justin, they need to change. They keep doing X, Y, and Z, and I hate it." That may be true. I won't disagree with you. But if you wait for them to make a change, which they won't, you give them a ton of power over you. If you wait around for them, they have power over your life, your emotions, maybe your wellbeing. I encourage you to take ownership over your wellbeing in all regards.

Hopefully this helps shift the dynamics in the relationship, and your spouse's nervous system picks up on it. Hopefully their nervous system then begins to shift, and that gets reinforced within the relationship. That is ultimately out of your control. What is in your control is what you do now to make a change. If you're honestly making changes and building more self-regulation, you'll be better able to ride the highs and the lows of the relationship.
I sincerely hope your loved one follows. If they refuse to better themselves and work on their own self-regulation, that is out of your control.
Let's talk about what you could do to start shifting the dynamics in your relationship. I have two general recommendations and two more specific things you can do.

Before you can co-regulate with someone, you must be able to self-regulate. Your most powerful tool is your own nervous system state. When that wave of anger comes from your partner, the work is to notice your own defensiveness rising, and instead of reacting from it, stay grounded in your own body, feeling your emotions and being with them while staying firmly anchored in safety. Ideally.

This is super hard. Some might say super duper hard. Mindfully connecting with the present moment through your senses? That's easy compared to this. Meditating for 30 minutes? No problem, compared to this. Self-regulating through someone else's emotional dysregulation? That's a challenge.

That doesn't mean you're happy. I don't expect you to smile through somebody else's anger. You can be upset, sad, angry too. But you need to be self-regulated while feeling those emotions. Not just in your behavior, though that's a great start, but in your emotions and in your biology too.

Someone who can hold back on the behavioral impulse to yell and swear and insult back at their spouse is off to a really great start. If that's you, keep it up. Great job. But someone who can notice and be with their anger while also connecting with their spouse's emotions is even further along. Again, not easy. And the person who can listen to their spouse's emotions without their own emotions getting triggered has a strong level of self-regulation.

I don't mean numbness. I don't mean not caring. I mean the ability to stay present and empathetic without your body losing access to its safety state. That's not a skill you learn overnight. It's something you practice. Again, super hard. So prioritize your self-regulation before, during, and after discussions with your partner.

blocks.h: Two: focus on small, consistent safety cues

blocks.p: You don't have to be perfect. You don't have to have long, drawn-out discussions that go until 2:00 a.m. with cathartic cries about childhood. It might be enough, for now, to intentionally make eye contact and smile when you mean it. Or to share a coffee together in the morning without any expectations. Or to bring up a happy memory out of the blue and laugh together. Or just to text that you're thinking of them, even though you're on the other side of the wall.

Small and spontaneous, without trying too hard, is good. But so is routine, so be predictable. When you say you're going to do something, do it. Do the boring stuff, like proactively cleaning up. Small, steady, predictable cues of safety.

blocks.h: Three: stop trying to fix your spouse

blocks.p: This one is counterintuitive. Of course you want to help. But the pressure to help can itself be a danger cue. It's not really a danger cue, but that person may interpret it as one.

"I want to prove that I can be her anchor." That energy, as well-intentioned as I'm sure it is, might feel intrusive to someone in shutdown. It can feel like a demand, even though you don't mean it that way. Like an expectation. Like one more thing that partner A is failing at.

Sometimes the most helpful thing you can do is less. Be present without an agenda. Exist nearby without requiring anything. Let them come to you, and accept them as they are now. Not how they treat you. As they are.

blocks.h: Four: validate the feeling, not necessarily the content

blocks.p: When anger does appear, you don't have to agree with the words being said to validate the emotion behind them. Instead of trying to defend yourself, try naming the feeling and even normalizing it, like "I can see why you're mad at me. I haven't been reliable," or "You felt let down when I (blank). I would probably feel disappointed too."

None of these tips, or countless more like them, are quick fixes. It's a slow and steady process to change ourselves, and also our relationships. So do your part in the relationship and be the gear that refuses to turn in an unhealthy and dysregulated way. Be as self-regulated as possible. And over time you will prove to your loved one that it's okay to soften their defenses. You can't control it, but over time you'll show it. Ideally, they're also working on themselves in some way.
If the relationship itself is the source of threat for your partner, you may not be able to be their anchor right now, or their co-regulator. That's not failure. That's reality.

She may need to build safety elsewhere first, like in individual therapy, or with friends, or through her own solo self-regulation practice. She may need to develop her own regulation before she can receive yours. Couples therapy might be indicated here as well, but not framed as fixing partner A. Framed more as: we're both going to work on this together, with professional support. It's an "us" issue, not a partner A issue.

You showing up differently is powerful, but it's not a guarantee at all. You could do everything right, and partner A may still need time, space, or outside support to find their way back to safety, and ultimately back to you.
Your job is not to drag that person out of shutdown. Your job is to become the kind of regulated presence that makes safety possible, if and when they're able to receive it.

So if you're partner B, the person trying to support a partner in shutdown, the work begins with you. It begins with your own regulation, your own capacity to be an anchor in the relationship storm. And it includes holding boundaries for yourself too, because your nervous system also matters.
